design_detail: Critical narrative review (written in honour of Oleh Hornykiewicz) comparing striatal dopamine markers, nigral cellularity, gliosis and parkinsonism risk in people who use methamphetamine with idiopathic Parkinson's disease as the reference pattern of dopamine neurone loss. Presented as a brief update of a 2014 book chapter by the first author. No search strategy, inclusion criteria or quantitative synthesis; the central evidence is the authors' own post-mortem, imaging and registry studies.
can_establish: How the dopamine-marker evidence in people who use methamphetamine (as cited) differs in pattern from Parkinson's disease, and which questions (nigral cell counts, structural terminal damage, gliosis) had not been studied in humans as of 2016.
cannot_establish: Whether methamphetamine damages dopamine neurones in humans (the authors say this is premature to conclude), the completeness of the evidence (no systematic search), or the size of any effect (no pooling or appraisal of the cited studies).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited post-mortem series: 20 people who used methamphetamine chronically and 14 controls of similar age and post-mortem interval, with 12 neuropathologically confirmed Parkinson's cases (Moszczynska et al., 2004, as summarized; section Methamphetamine users: One (Toronto) laboratory reports low brain dopamine).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; studies chosen by the authors.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence selection is the authors' own; most of the human evidence discussed in detail comes from their laboratory (post-mortem dopamine and markers, VMAT2 PET, glial markers) or their registry collaboration (California hospital cohort). The cited post-mortem users had all used methamphetamine within about 5 days of death, so post-mortem findings describe recent use, not abstinence.

exposure.measurement: Varies across cited studies. In the authors' post-mortem series, use was confirmed by methamphetamine and/or amphetamine in blood and brain at autopsy; amounts and duration of use are not given in this review.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed for the cited studies.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Post-mortem series: last use within about 5 days of death. Imaging studies cited range from early abstinence (under 1 week; 7–15 days) to a reputed 3 years.

comparison.controls: Parkinson's disease as the reference dopamine-deficiency disorder; non-using controls of the cited studies.
comparison.matching: Post-mortem controls of similar age and post-mortem interval (as summarized).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use data in any cited human study.

outcomes.instruments: Cited measures: striatal dopamine (HPLC with electrochemical detection), metabolites (HVA, DOPAC, 3-MT), synthetic enzymes (tyrosine hydroxylase, dopa decarboxylase), VMAT2 (radioligand binding, immunohistochemistry, [11C]dihydrotetrabenazine PET), DAT (binding, Western blot, PET/SPECT), substantia nigra cellularity (qualitative), glial markers (PET [11C]PK11195; immunohistochemistry; Western blot), diagnosed Parkinson's disease in registry cohorts.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors argue that every dopamine marker can be up- or down-regulated independently of the number of terminals (a biochemical marker confound), so no marker loss can be equated with loss of neuropil (Conclusions, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Damage is framed as loss of whole dopamine neurones or terminals; its signature is taken to be reduction of all dopamine markers together, as in Parkinson's disease.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited (Dopamine section; Clinical parkinsonism section). Post-mortem striatal dopamine in methamphetamine users: 61% lower in caudate and 50% lower in putamen than controls, most individual users below the control range; Parkinson's disease: 82% (caudate) and 97% (putamen) lower, no overlap with controls. Two individual users had 95% and 97% caudate dopamine loss. VMAT2: about 10% lower in one PET study of users reputedly abstinent 3 years; higher in early abstinence (under 1 week) and normal at 7–15 days in two PET studies from the authors' group. [11C]PK11195 binding 250–1500% higher in one PET study, with uncertain quantification. Parkinson's disease risk: California hospital cohort followed up to 16 years, hazard ratio 1.76 (95% CI 1.12–2.75) vs an appendicitis comparison group, no increase in a cocaine group; Utah population database, HR 2.8 (95% CI 1.6–4.8).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection; the counter-evidence from animal neurotoxicity is summarized in a few sentences with references to the 2014 chapter. The registry studies are presented as consistent with damage in a small subgroup, without discussion of their confounding.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the authors' post-mortem series of recent users, striatal dopamine and DAT were low while dopamine metabolites, synthetic enzymes and VMAT2 were normal; in Parkinson's disease all markers are low and putamen loss exceeds caudate loss. No quantitative nigral counts or structural terminal studies exist in human users; gliosis findings are mixed; two registry cohorts report higher Parkinson's disease risk.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The review explicitly concludes it is premature to say whether recreational methamphetamine causes or does not cause dopamine neurone loss, and labels its further views (no significant neurone damage at the doses their subjects used; dopamine depletion from acute release, partly reversible; DAT reduction as compensatory down-regulation without neurone loss) as speculation (Conclusions). The abstract goes a step further in proposing that the striatal dopamine deficiency could in principle be corrected by dopamine substitution, although the deficiency rests on one unreplicated post-mortem series of people who had used within days of death and on VMAT2 imaging in early abstinence; the body adds that levodopa should probably not be given while methamphetamine is present and that the deficiency may be short-lived. The marker-pattern argument against neurone loss depends on the stability of the very markers the authors say can be regulated independently of neurone number.

timeline.event: Toronto post-mortem study (Wilson et al., 1996, as described in this review): striatal DAT reduced by binding and Western blot; dopamine metabolites, synthetic enzymes and VMAT2 normal.
First PET report of lower striatal DAT binding in abstinent methamphetamine users (McCann et al., 1998; appraised in this batch).
PET study of 15 users vs 18 controls, cited by Kish as Volkow et al., 2001b
Follow-up PET suggesting DAT normalizes with protracted abstinence, cited by Kish as Volkow et al., 2001a
Toronto post-mortem series summarized: 20 users, 14 controls, 12 Parkinson's cases; dopamine 61% (caudate) and 50% (putamen) lower in users (Moszczynska et al., 2004, as described in this review).
California hospital cohort: higher Parkinson's disease incidence after methamphetamine/amphetamine-related hospitalization
Utah population database: higher Parkinson's disease risk, HR 2.8 as cited by Kish
VMAT2 PET in early abstinence from the same group: binding raised in the first days and normal by 7–15 days (Boileau et al., 2016; appraised in this batch).
Meta-analysis pooling DAT studies in amphetamine-type users, g −1.47 (Ashok et al., 2017; appraised in this batch).

replication.where_it_stands: The DAT reduction is well replicated; whether it reflects terminal loss is unresolved. Post-mortem low dopamine in recent users still awaits independent replication (the authors call it preliminary). Nigral cell counts and structural terminal pathology have not been studied in human users.

funding.funder: US National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIH) grants DA07182 and DA040066 to S.J.K. (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the author manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto, and the University of Northern British Columbia. Much of the evidence discussed in detail is the authors' own (post-mortem series, VMAT2 PET, glial markers, California registry cohort); Kish and Boileau are authors of the Boileau 2016 VMAT2 study and Kish and Callaghan of the California registry study. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Quantitative stereological counts of nigral dopamine neurones and structural studies of striatal dopamine terminals (with several markers) in post-mortem brains of long-term users with known abstinence, against matched controls; independent replication of the low post-mortem dopamine finding; and longitudinal PET of DAT and VMAT2 in the same users through sustained abstinence.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; the authors chose the evidence.
No formal appraisal, though some limitations are named (uncertain PK11195 quantification; post-mortem dopamine finding unreplicated).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Post-mortem, VMAT2, glial and registry evidence is largely from the authors' group.
Speculations are labelled as such in the Conclusions.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against damage
domains.note: Animal neurotoxicity evidence summarized only briefly; registry studies discussed without their confounding.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3 lists none). The review is explicit about uncertainty and labels speculation, but its selection is unsystematic and weighted toward the authors' own studies. Claims should cite the primary studies it summarizes, using this review for the argument about marker patterns and the list of unstudied questions.

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude it is premature, on the available literature, to say whether recreational methamphetamine does or does not cause loss of or damage to dopamine neurones in humans.

Post-mortem striatal dopamine (authors' series: 20 users with use within about 5 days of death, 14 controls): 61% lower in caudate and 50% lower in putamen; most individual users below the control range. In 12 Parkinson's cases: 82% (caudate) and 97% (putamen) lower, with no overlap with controls.
key_findings.locator: Dopamine › Methamphetamine users: One (Toronto) laboratory reports low brain dopamine, 2nd–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In the same post-mortem users, striatal HVA, DOPAC, 3-MT, tyrosine hydroxylase and dopa decarboxylase were normal, whereas all are reduced in Parkinson's disease; the authors read this as little support for marked loss of whole dopamine neurones.

Striatal DAT is reduced in methamphetamine users post-mortem (binding and Western blot; also immunohistochemistry in a Japanese series) and in imaging studies from seven independent groups; the authors call it the most replicated dopamine-marker finding and state its cause (transporter regulation vs neurone loss) is still argued, with imaging suggesting it can normalize with extended abstinence.

VMAT2: normal post-mortem (one study; a second showed a non-significant trend lower in accumbens and putamen); about 10% lower by PET in users reputedly abstinent 3 years (Johanson et al., 2006, at a low non-saturating tracer dose); raised in early abstinence (under 1 week) and normal at 7–15 days in two PET studies from the authors' group, explained as less competition from low vesicular dopamine.
key_findings.note: Ashok et al. (2017) describe the Johanson study as after three months of abstinence with a significant reduction; the two reviews disagree on its abstinence duration.

key_findings.finding: No quantitative counts of nigral dopamine cell bodies exist in human methamphetamine users; a neuropathologist's qualitative review of the authors' cases found no obvious nigral cell loss.
key_findings.locator: Substantia Nigra Cellularity › Methamphetamine users section

key_findings.finding: Gliosis evidence is limited to three studies with mixed results: a PET study with 250–1500% higher [11C]PK11195 binding (quantification uncertain), a post-mortem study with normal or increased microglial and normal astroglial counts, and the authors' study with normal intact glial proteins but increased degraded HSP-27 and vimentin.
key_findings.locator: Brain Gliosis › Methamphetamine users: Brain gliosis status is uncertain

key_findings.finding: Registry evidence cited: California hospital cohort (follow-up up to 16 years), HR 1.76 (95% CI 1.12–2.75) for Parkinson's disease vs an appendicitis group, cocaine group not elevated, cited jointly to Callaghan et al. (2010) and Callaghan et al. (2012a), both co-authored by Kish, without saying which of the two reports the figure; Utah database HR 2.8 (95% CI 1.6–4.8). The authors call these consistent with damage in a subgroup but not proof, and note only a very small proportion of users are later diagnosed.
key_findings.locator: Does Methamphetamine Cause Clinical Parkinsonism in the Human?, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Pattern differences: dopamine loss in users was greater in caudate than putamen, the reverse of Parkinson's disease; the summary table lists dopamine and DAT as decreased in users, metabolites and synthetic enzymes as normal, VMAT2 as normal to slightly decreased, and nigral cellularity as unknown.

In the authors' VMAT2 study, higher striatal VMAT2 binding went with poorer performance on some neuropsychological tests, but users showed only slight cognitive deficits relative to controls overall; a separate study found amphetamine-induced D3/D2 binding changes enhanced or unchanged, not blunted, in users abstinent at least 7 days.
key_findings.locator: Comment › Marked dopamine loss could be harmful, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that any dopamine marker can change without a change in terminal number, so quantitative marker losses cannot be equated with loss of dopamine neuropil, and that structural terminal damage has not been examined in post-mortem brain of users.

Two people in the authors' post-mortem series had near-total caudate dopamine loss (95% and 97%), which the authors place in the 'Parkinsonian range'; they think these two probably had some behavioural impairment from it, and suspect that the main dopamine-related harm in people who use methamphetamine would be cognitive, lasting while the deficiency is severe. No behavioural data are reported.
key_findings.locator: Comment › Marked dopamine loss could be harmful, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The authors' inference from two cases of Moszczynska et al. (2004); the next paragraph adds that a link between low dopamine and cognitive deficits remains to be established.

reporting_issues.issue: Kish et al. label the 2001 Volkow papers in reverse order to this project's ids: their Volkow 2001a is the J Neurosci recovery follow-up (project id volkow_2001b) and their 2001b is the Am J Psychiatry 15-vs-18 study (project id volkow_2001a).
reporting_issues.consequence: Risk of mis-citation when claims are cross-referenced; use the DOI.

reporting_issues.issue: The text counts seven independent PET/SPECT imaging studies but cites ten papers (from seven first-author groups), including Schouw et al. (2013), which studied recreational dexamphetamine users rather than methamphetamine users.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Dopamine Transporter › Methamphetamine users: Why?)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the number of methamphetamine-specific groups is six or seven depending on how that study is counted.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists VMAT2 among markers not below normal in users, while the table gives normal to slightly decreased and the text cites a 10% PET reduction.

Kish describes Johanson et al. (2006) as users reputedly abstinent 3 years with 10% lower VMAT2 binding; Ashok et al. (2017) describe the same study as 3 months' abstinence with a large reduction (g 1.68).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cross-review inconsistency; the primary paper must be read before either description is cited.
